study.title: 2 Samuel 5 - David is confirmed as king of all Israel, and overcomes the Philistines
study.overview: The chapter shows the consolidation of David's reign in three main movements: the tribes of Israel recognize him as king and he is anointed over all the people; Jerusalem is taken and becomes the city of David; and the Lord grants him victories over the Philistines when David inquires of God before acting. The text highlights that David's ascension is not merely a political result, but is linked to God's choice, divine direction and the king's practical obedience. At the same time, the chapter also records the expansion of his home and the emergence of future tensions, as David takes more women and concubines.

outline.title: The tribes recognize David as king
outline.explanation: After the death of Ishbosheth and the end of Saul's house resistance, the elders of Israel go to Hebron, confess blood ties with David, and remember that the Lord had already chosen him to shepherd the people. David makes a covenant before the Lord, and he is anointed king over all Israel. The text also records the duration of his government, first in Hebron and then in Jerusalem.

outline.title: The seizure of Jerusalem and the affirmation of the city of David
outline.explanation: David conquers the fortress of Zion, casts out the arrogant trust of the Jebusites and established his residence there. He fortifies the city and receives the summary statement of its prosperity: it grew because the Lord of hosts was with him. The city is now known as the city of David.

outline.title: Palace, confirmation and growth of David's house
outline.explanation: Hiram of Tyre sends materials and workers to the construction of the house of David, which shows the external recognition of his reign. David understands that the Lord had confirmed him as king because of the people. Then the chapter mentions that he takes more concubines and women and generates sons and daughters in Jerusalem, listing their names.

outline.title: The two campaigns against the Philistines
outline.explanation: The Philistines go up against David, but he inquires of the Lord before fighting. In the first battle, David interprets victory as a divine breakup of enemies and even the idols abandoned by the Philistines are burned. When the Philistines return, David consults the Lord again and receives specific instructions; obeying exactly, defeats them from Gibeah to Gaza.

study.context: The chapter fits the moment the inner division of Israel is shut down and David proceeds to rule all the people. The text itself and the notes indicate that the death of Isbosete and Abner opened the way for David's acceptance by the elders of the northern tribes. Hebron appears as the early stage of his reign in Judah, while Jerusalem becomes the new capital. The notes also note that the conquest of Jerusalem was especially significant because the city was linked to the region of Benjamin and the Jebusites. There is not enough basis here to detail external dates or historical reconstructions beyond what the chapter states.
study.theology: The chapter presents the sovereignty of God in the formation of the kingdom. David is not just a skilled leader; he is the chosen king and confirmed by the Lord. The language of pastor and prince shows that government, in the biblical perspective, involves care and direction of the people, not only authority. The covenant made in Hebron reinforces that David's reign is under the gaze of God and before him. In Jerusalem, David's prosperity is explicitly attributed to the presence of the Lord of hosts, and military victory comes after humble consultation and concrete obedience. At the same time, the text does not idealize the king: the mention of more concubines and women points to moral complexities and to a large royal family that will have consequences in the later biblical narrative. The chapter also contrasts the confidence of the Philistines in their idols with the living action of the Lord, who breaks the enemies and guides his people.

scholarViews.insight: The northern tribes recognize David after the death of Abner and Isbosete, and the text emphasizes that they receive him as their king because they already knew of the choice of God and his role as a pastor of the people.
The victory in Baal-Perazim is described as the Lord's work, so that David correctly interprets success as divine intervention against the Philistines.
David obeys precisely the instructions received from the Lord in the second battle, and this obedience is highlighted as the reason for the success of the campaign.

questions: What changes when the people officially recognize the leadership that God had already indicated?
Why does the text insist so much on David consult the Lord before fighting?
How is David's prosperity presented as a gift of God and not as mere human merit?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to seek God's direction before making important decisions, rather than acting only by impulse or self-tership. He also calls humility in remembering that real victories come from the Lord, not just human abilities. In practice, this means praying with sincerity, obeying what has already been revealed in the Scriptures and recognize what positions, resources, and results are entrusted by God for the good of his people. The text also warns of the danger of growing externally and, at the same time, making room for family and personal choices that displease the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explain in detail the mechanics of the conquest of Jerusalem, and the notes present possibilities without consensus, so it is not possible to affirm with certainty how David entered the city. Nor is there a secure basis in this chapter to define with historical precision the meaning of certain place names or to build detailed conclusions about David's family life beyond what the text declares. The readings of the commentators are interpretative and, in some points, only likely, not conclusive.
